City mushroomsGBIF chanterelle records were counted in grid cells of about 110 km (1° × 1.5°). Each cell's count goes to the largest city (40,000+ people) within about 110 km. Mushroom size follows that total, so it means "forests around the city", not the city itself. Estimated.
Rain contoursMonthly rain normals from 86 weather stations (mostly 1991–2020), summed for the chosen month or season and blended between stations (weighted by distance, about 180 km reach). Areas more than 450 km from a station stay blank. Estimated.
Fox's bagTap a spot or a city mushroom. The bag fills in proportion to that place's records in the chosen month, compared with its busiest month. The tag shows the actual record count.

Species

Two golden chanterelles.

One across Europe, one along the Pacific coast of North America.

Europe

Golden chanterelle

Cantharellus cibarius
Forest
Conifer and broadleaf (spruce, pine, oak, beech and others)
Season
June–December, peak August–September
Records
About 80% of Europe's Cantharellus records
Pacific Northwest

Pacific golden chanterelle

Cantharellus formosus
Forest
Douglas-fir, western hemlock, spruce (40–60-year-old second growth)
Season
July–December, peak mid-September to October
Split
Separated from C. cibarius in 1997; told apart by DNA

How to recognise one: blunt, forking ridges (false gills) run down the stem instead of sharp blade-like gills, and it grows from soil. The toxic jack-o'-lantern looks similar. Check with a local expert before eating anything you pick.

Model plan

From last season's weather to this year's bag.

Four steps from records and weather to a monthly chance of finding chanterelles.

Grid × month

Split each region into 25 km cells and label every cell and month as "records" or "no records".

Inputs

Rain, temperature and soil moisture for the previous 1–6 months, plus forest type, soil pH, elevation and month.

Models

Logistic regression, then XGBoost, then an LSTM or 1D-CNN. Europe and North America trained separately.

Validation

Train on earlier years, test on recent ones. Use counts of other fungi records to correct for how often people visit a cell.
